evidence.claim: A former wagon route links Lake Superior, forest and five waterfalls
evidence.quote: The route of the byway first existed as a wagon road in the 1840s

evidence.claim: A former wagon route links Lake Superior, forest and five waterfalls
evidence.quote: The Black River Scenic Byway begins northwest of Bessemer, Michigan, at the intersection of CR 204 (Airport Road) and CR 513 (Black River Road) and continues for 11 miles to Black River Harbor.

evidence.claim: A former wagon route links Lake Superior, forest and five waterfalls
evidence.quote: The road provides access to five sets of waterfalls.

evidence.claim: Black River Scenic Byway follows County Road 513 through pine, hemlock and hardwood forest between Airport Road and Black River Harbor.
evidence.quote: The woods through which the roadway passes contain pine, hemlock, and hardwood trees.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service describes an 11-mile drive and credits its scenery and recreation opportunities for the byway’s 1992 dedication.
evidence.quote: continues for 11 miles to Black River Harbor. Officially dedicated as a National Scenic Byway on September 19, 1992, for its exceptional beauty, recreational beauty and recreational opportunities.

evidence.claim: The road runs west of the Black River, back from its banks, with trails leading to five waterfalls.
evidence.quote: CR 513 runs along the western side of the river, staying shy of the banks as it passes through the woods.

evidence.claim: A wagon road recorded in William A. Burt’s 1848 surveys connected the harbor site with Chippewa Hill, now the location of Copper Peak.
evidence.quote: According to the surveys of William A. Burt in 1848, a wagon road ran south from the modern site of the Black River Harbor to Chippewa Hill, the location of Copper Peak.

evidence.claim: Michigan built a waterfront-to-Bessemer wagon road in 1904; a county road followed by 1927.
evidence.quote: A wagon road was built by the State of Michigan in 1904 to connect the waterfront with Bessemer.

evidence.claim: Local officials proposed National Forest Scenic Byway status in 1991, and the Forest Service conferred it in June 1992.
evidence.quote: Local officials originally proposed the National Forest Scenic Byway designation for the road in April 1991.

evidence.claim: Traveling south from Lake Superior, begin at Black River Harbor and work inland past access to Rainbow, Sandstone, Gorge, Potawatomi and Great Conglomerate Falls.
evidence.quote: The first is Great Conglomerate Falls, followed by Potawatomi, Gorge, Sandstone, and Rainbow Falls.

evidence.claim: Copper Peak comes next, where the road curves away from the river.
evidence.quote: The byway curves away from the river near Copper Peak

evidence.claim: Continue through the forest to Airport Road, the designated drive’s southern end; County Road 513 carries on toward US 2 near Bessemer.
evidence.quote: While CR 513 (Black River Road) extends further south to connect with US Highway 2 near Bessemer, the National Forest Scenic Byway designation starts at the intersection with CR 204 (Airport Road)

evidence.claim: Black River Scenic Byway follows County Road 513
evidence.quote: The byway follows County Road 513 (CR 513)

evidence.claim: Traveling south from Lake Superior, begin at Black River Harbor
evidence.quote: The Black River Harbor Recreation Area Picnic area overlooks the Black River as it runs into the harbor and on into Lake Superior.

evidence.claim: A wooden suspension bridge carries the North Country Trail across the Black River at the harbor.
evidence.quote: The trail parallels the Black River for most of the journey north from Copper Peak, crosses the Black River on the suspension bridge, and then continues east toward the Porcupine Mountains Wilderness State Park.

evidence.claim: The crossing also leads to a trail reaching Lake Superior’s sand-and-stone shoreline.
evidence.quote: The shoreline is a natural mixture of sand and stone. The natural shoreline is accessed by crossing the famous wooden suspension bridge and then following the trail to the water.

evidence.claim: The harbor occupies the site of a 1920s fishing village.
evidence.quote: The harbor is the site of a 1920s fishing village

evidence.claim: In 1967, Gogebic County exchanged its riverside park land, including the harbor, with the Forest Service.
evidence.quote: In 1967, the Gogebic County exchanged the park land along the river, including the harbor, with the USFS for other land in the area

evidence.claim: A historic pavilion built by the Civilian Conservation Corps overlooks the harbor, lake and picnic area.
evidence.quote: A historic pavilion built by the Civilian Conservation Corps is also located here.

evidence.claim: overlooks the harbor, lake and picnic area.
evidence.quote: This historic building sits overlooking the Black River Harbor, Lake Superior and the picnic area.

evidence.claim: The wooden suspension bridge leads toward a shoreline of sand and stone.
evidence.quote: The shoreline is a natural mixture of sand and stone. The natural shoreline is accessed by crossing the famous wooden suspension bridge and then following the trail to the water.

evidence.claim: Winter access to the day-use area and waterfall trailheads can be limited by snow plowing; services are reduced.
evidence.quote: The day use area and waterfall trailheads are open year-round; however, services are reduced, and winter access can be limited due to snow plowing.

evidence.claim: A large conglomerate outcrop divides Great Conglomerate Falls in the middle of the Black River.
evidence.quote: The falls takes its name from the large conglomerate outcropping in the middle of the river that forms its segmented appearance.

evidence.claim: The waterfall drops 30 feet; when summer water is lower, it separates into two drops.
evidence.quote: Great Conglomerate Falls is a 30 feet (9.1 m) waterfall on the Black River in Michigan. It is split into two drops in the summertime when water is lower.

evidence.claim: Its name comes from that outcrop.
evidence.quote: The falls takes its name from the large conglomerate outcrop

evidence.claim: This is the southernmost of the five waterfall stops on the byway, before Copper Peak when traveling inland.
evidence.quote: North of Copper Peak

evidence.claim: The Forest Service describes short trails from paved parking lots to the waterfalls, with steps on most paths.
evidence.quote: You can take any of the five short (1/4 - 3/4 mile) trails to the waterfalls, which are all accessible from paved parking lots.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service reports major repairs to waterfall platforms and trails.
evidence.quote: Black River Waterfall Platforms and Trails Undergoing Major Repairs

evidence.claim: Copper Peak’s ski-slide and tower stand above a hill where mining failed to produce copper.
evidence.quote: The Copper Peak ski-slide and tower dominates the peak of the hill.

evidence.claim: The Chippewa Copper Mining Company began work in 1845, driving a tunnel into the rock, but produced no copper and closed.
evidence.quote: In 1845, the Chippewa Copper Mining Company began mining work here, sinking a tunnel into the granite rock. They produced no copper and eventually closed.

evidence.claim: The 1845 tunnel and excavation pits remain visible on the hill.
evidence.quote: An 1845 tunnel and several copper excavation pits are visible on the hill

evidence.claim: Ski flying competitions began in 1970, with ten FIS-sanctioned competitions held through 1994.
evidence.quote: Between 1970 and 1994 there were ten competitions sanctioned by FIS

evidence.claim: Landing-hill reconstruction was underway by May 2025, with completion scheduled for December 2026.
evidence.quote: As of May 2025, reconstruction of the landing hill has begun and is the construction of the concrete ski jump landing hill and outrun is scheduled to be complete in December 2026.

evidence.claim: The county had purchased waterfront land for a park in 1924. Fishing-village residents were forced to move and settled at Black River Village.
evidence.quote: The county had purchased the land around the waterfront in 1924 for a park, and a county road running parallel to the Black River was in place by 1927. The residents of the fishing village were forced to move and settled at Black River Village.

evidence.claim: After crossing the river, the North Country Trail continues east toward Porcupine Mountains Wilderness State Park.
evidence.quote: crosses the Black River on the suspension bridge, and then continues east toward the Porcupine Mountains Wilderness State Park.

evidence.claim: Inside the pavilion are tables and a fireplace.
evidence.quote: It has flush toilets, tables and a fireplace inside.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service attributes the river’s color to tannin from hemlock trees.
evidence.quote: Tannin (tannic acids) from hemlock trees is what gives it its unique color.

evidence.claim: The ski tower rests on concrete footings set in solid rock; its construction did not disturb the earlier tunnel and excavation pits.
evidence.quote: The tower sits on concrete footings based in solid rock. An 1845 tunnel and several copper excavation pits are visible on the hill, and are not affected by the construction of the ski-slide.
